\section{Conclusion and open interface}\label{sec:conclusion}

The affine recurrence action turns one weak MCFL pumping family into a
single injective numerical orbit with simultaneous local returns. Positive
pumped length and uniqueness of canonical representation supply
distinctness, while finite-group return times supply congruences. Applying
Broughan's adic classifications to these orbits,
together with the deleted-prime intrinsic derivative calculation, gives the
scattered-set obstruction, the nonunit escape dichotomy, and prime and
bounded-\(\Omega\) MCF-immunity.

For the minimal tail recurrence, the residual bounded-support phenomenon
has an exact structural form. It occurs on an infinite finite-fan-out MCFL
if and only if the canonical language contains a synchronized ray with
values \(cb^t\). Evertse's quotient theorem is used with an explicit
prime-ideal norm bound to reduce a fixed-support recurrence to one
characteristic root; Schur's theorem removes its polynomial factor. The
ratio \(b\) uses only primes dividing the minimal tail constant. In a
standard greedy linear numeration basis with weak-Perron recurrence, residue
asymptotics and length thresholds show that such a ray exists exactly when
some positive power of the weak Perron number is an integer. Alternating
radices give an infinite family with nonintegral root \(\sqrt B\) and a
regular ray of values \(B^t\).

On the promised class of valid effectively presented regular canonical
systems, with the minimal tail recurrence and threshold supplied or
certified, positive promised instances can be enumerated and certified. The unresolved general step is not
candidate verification but witness compression: no computable bound is
known for the fan-out and word lengths of a smallest geometric synchronized
scheme. DFA path compression does not preserve the associated affine
recurrence matrices. Conversely, no reduction proving undecidability is
known that also preserves unique canonical representation, the minimal tail
recurrence, and the special digit-matrix form.
Accordingly the general decision problem remains open, while the
weak-Perron subclass has the exact algebraic classification above.

The nearest broader global problem is the degeneracy/Cobham-extension
problem for context-free sequences discussed by Caucal and Le Gonidec
\cite{CaucalLeGonidec2014}; this paper does not settle it. The weak pumping
mechanism itself still supplies only one ray inside one infinite MCFL, and
two representations of the same set may supply unrelated rays with no
common values. It neither controls every sufficiently long word nor the
whole canonical language. The slender-context-free theorem proved here
escapes that ceiling only because the Latteux--Thierrin--Ilie
classification replaces a single pumped orbit by a finite paired-loop cover
of each full representation language. Mignotte's theorem then makes every
pair of loop images have finite intersection. Retaining the individual
recurrence shifts, spectral data, and effective Mignotte thresholds gives the
cardinality bound in \Cref{thm:effective-slender-cfl-cardinality}, but not a
closed bound in compact grammar-size parameters. This is a different global
argument, not a strengthening of the weak MCFL pumping lemma.

The Supplementary Information (Online Resource 1) contains the independent fixed-DFA density and
regular Zeckendorf results. Keeping those comparisons outside the article
leaves the main theorem chain centered on synchronized recurrence orbits
and their arithmetic consequences.

We submit "Prime support and multiple-context-free languages in recurrent
numeration" for consideration as an Original Research Article in Monatshefte
fuer Mathematik.

The article studies prime-support obstructions for canonical languages in
eventually recurrent numeration systems. Its main results combine weak
multiple-context-free pumping with the affine recurrence action, adic
topology, and recurrence arithmetic. The manuscript is mathematically
self-contained; none of its theorem proofs depends on a numbered result in
the Supplementary Information.

online resources be made available to the referees with the main manuscript.

\begin{proof}
  Choose a sufficiently long word in \(L\) and apply
  \Cref{thm:context-free-coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping}. Since
  \(N_j\mid N_i\) for \(j\le i\), while every \(Q_i>1\) is coprime to
  \(N_i\), a prime divisor of \(Q_i\) divides no earlier value. Thus
  \(\omega(N_i)\ge\omega(N_0)+i\). The immunity conclusions follow
  exactly as in the regular cases: \(\omega\le K\) on \(\mathcal B_K\),
  \(\mathcal A_K\subseteq\mathcal B_K\), and
  \(\omega\le\abs S\) on \(\mathcal Z_S\). Finally prime values have
  \(\omega=1\), while Euclid's theorem makes
  \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal Z}\) infinite.
\end{proof}

We next isolate the precise base-independent interface. This is
deliberately narrower than every object called a Pisot or abstract
numeration system in the literature.

\begin{definition}[Canonical eventually recurrent numeration]
  \label{def:canonical-eventually-recurrent-numeration}
  A canonical eventually recurrent numeration system consists of:
  \begin{enumerate}[label={}]
    \item[\textup{(U1)}] a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers
    \(U=(U_n)_{n\ge0}\) and a finite digit alphabet
    \(A\subseteq\NN\) containing \(0\);
    \item[\textup{(U2)}] an LSD-first language
    \(\mathcal R_U\subseteq A^\ast\), with
    \[
      \val_U(x_0\cdots x_{m-1})
        :=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}x_jU_j,
    \]
    for which \(\val_U:\mathcal R_U\to\NN_{\ge1}\) is a bijection;
    \item[\textup{(U4)}] integers \(J\ge0,d\ge1,a_0,\ldots,a_{d-1}\), with
    \(a_0\ne0\), such that
    \[
      U_{n+d}=a_0U_n+a_1U_{n+1}+\cdots+a_{d-1}U_{n+d-1}
      \qquad(n\ge J).
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
  Relative to this recurrence witness, it is a \emph{unit system} if
  \(\abs{a_0}=1\). No regularity of \(\mathcal R_U\) is included in
  this definition, and no comparison between the values of canonical words
  of different lengths is assumed. The label \textup{(U4)} is retained to
  preserve the numbering of the recurrence hypothesis used throughout.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Affine recurrence block action]
  \label{lem:affine-recurrence-block-action}
  Under \textup{(U4)}, let \(C\) be the \(d\times d\) companion matrix
  with superdiagonal entries \(1\) and last row
  \((a_0,\ldots,a_{d-1})\). For \(\varepsilon\in A\), put
  \[
    D_\varepsilon=
    \begin{pmatrix}
      1&\varepsilon e_1^t\\
      0&C
    \end{pmatrix}.
  \]
  Once \(r\ge J\), appending \(\varepsilon\) sends
  \[
    (N_r,U_r,\ldots,U_{r+d-1})^t
    \quad\hbox{to}\quad
    D_\varepsilon(N_r,U_r,\ldots,U_{r+d-1})^t.
  \]
  Moreover
  \(\det D_\varepsilon=(-1)^{d-1}a_0\). Hence every block action is
  invertible modulo \(q\) whenever \(\gcd(q,a_0)=1\), and modulo every
  \(q\ge2\) in a unit system. Here and below, for a block
  \(b=b_1\cdots b_\ell\), we write
  \(M_b=D_{b_\ell}\cdots D_{b_1}\), with \(M_\varepsilon=I\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
  The first coordinate becomes \(N_r+\varepsilon U_r\); the remaining
  coordinates shift once and the final one is supplied by \textup{(U4)}.
  These are exactly the displayed matrix equations. The determinant
  is \(\det C=(-1)^{d-1}a_0\). Multiplicativity of determinants gives
  the assertion for blocks.
\end{proof}

The coefficient \(a_0\) belongs to the displayed recurrence witness,
not intrinsically to \((U,A,\mathcal R_U)\); see
\Cref{prop:recurrence-witness-separation} for the resulting strict
separation.

We now use the standard fan-out convention: a multiple context-free
language (MCFL) is a \(k\)-MCFL for some finite \(k\ge1\). An infinite
language is \emph{MCF-immune} if it contains no infinite MCFL
sublanguage. The weak pumping lemma of Seki--Matsumura--Fujii--Kasami
states that an infinite \(k\)-MCFL contains one word that can be pumped
synchronously at \(2k\) factors \cite[Lemma~3.2]{SekiEtAl1991}. The
  lemma makes no assertion about every sufficiently long word; that
  stronger form fails for general MCFLs
  \cite{KanazawaKobeleMichaelisSalvatiYoshinaka2014}.

  Duncan--Elder--Frenkel--Lyu's substitution lemma
  \cite[Theorem~4.5]{DuncanElderFrenkelLiu2026} is stronger in a different
  quantifier direction: after enough positions of each sufficiently long
  word are marked, it gives either a bounded pump or a factorization in
  which a tuple can be replaced by another tuple from one of finitely many
  switchable families. It does not select a single family parameterized by
  one exponent \(t\), nor does it make all replacement blocks simultaneous
  powers of fixed words. Consequently it supplies neither a fixed affine
  matrix-power expression nor a return time valid for every parameter on
  one orbit. The switchable alternative also prevents it from replacing the
  paired Ogden pump in the Zeckendorf argument above. Thus it does not by
  itself imply any immunity result proved here. We use Seki et al.'s weaker
  conclusion precisely because its one synchronized family has the fixed
  \(2k\)-block power form needed below. The imported language statement is
  only that family; its placement beyond the recurrence transient, the
  finite-group return, and all arithmetic consequences are proved here.

\begin{theorem}[Synchronized local-congruence orbit]
  \label{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}
  Let \((U,A,\mathcal R_U)\) satisfy \textup{(U1)}, \textup{(U2)}, and
  \textup{(U4)}, and let
  \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) be an infinite \(k\)-MCFL. There are words
  \[
    \begin{gathered}
      a,u_1,\ldots,u_{k+1},v_1,\ldots,v_k\in A^\ast,\\
      w_1,\ldots,w_k,s_1,\ldots,s_k\in A^\ast
    \end{gathered}
  \]
  such that
  \[
    W(t)=a u_1v_1^tw_1s_1^tu_2\cdots
          u_kv_k^tw_ks_k^tu_{k+1}\in L
          \qquad(t\ge0),
  \]
  \[
    \sum_{j=1}^k(\abs{v_j}+\abs{s_j})>0,
  \]
  and the positive integers \(N(t):=\val_U(W(t))\) are pairwise distinct.
  Moreover, for
  every \(q\ge2\) with \(\gcd(q,a_0)=1\), there is \(H(q)\ge1\) such
  that
  \[
    N(t+H(q))\equiv N(t)\pmod q
    \qquad\text{for every }t\ge0.
  \]
  The factorization, and hence the orbit \(W(t)\), is independent of
  \(q\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  Put \(L^{\ge J}=L\cap A^{\ge J}\). This is still an infinite
  \(k\)-MCFL: its complement in \(L\) is finite because \(A\) is finite,
  and intersection with the regular language \(A^{\ge J}\) preserves
  \(k\)-MCFLs. Some \(a\in A^J\) is the prefix of infinitely many words
  of \(L^{\ge J}\); when \(J=0\), take \(a=\varepsilon\). For completeness,
  fixed left quotient preserves fan-out. Introduce a fresh letter \(\#\),
  let \(h(\#)=a\) and \(h(x)=x\) for \(x\in A\), intersect
  \(h^{-1}(L)\) with the regular language \(\#A^*\), and erase \(\#\).
  Inverse homomorphism, regular intersection, and homomorphism preserve
  \(k\)-MCFLs without increasing the maximum nonterminal dimension
  \cite[Proposition~2.3]{DuncanElderFrenkelLiu2026}. Hence
  \[
    L_a=\{x\in A^\ast:ax\in L\}
  \]
  is an infinite \(k\)-MCFL. The weak pumping lemma supplies
  \(u_j,v_j,w_j,s_j\) with the displayed synchronized pumping property
  and with at least one \(v_j\) or \(s_j\) nonempty.

  All digit actions after \(a\) are in the stationary range of
  \textup{(U4)}. Fix an allowed modulus \(q\). By
  \Cref{lem:affine-recurrence-block-action}, every nonempty matrix among
  \[
    M_{v_1},M_{s_1},\ldots,M_{v_k},M_{s_k}
  \]
  lies in the finite group
  \(\operatorname{GL}_{d+1}(\ZZ/q\ZZ)\). One may take
  \[
    H(q)=\abs{\operatorname{GL}_{d+1}(\ZZ/q\ZZ)}
      \le q^{(d+1)^2};
  \]
  Lagrange's theorem makes this a common multiple of their orders, and
  empty blocks contribute the identity.
  Replacing \(t\) by \(t+H(q)\) in the matrix product for \(W(t)\)
  therefore leaves every powered block unchanged modulo \(q\), proving
  the congruence simultaneously for all \(t\ge0\).

  Finally,
  \[
    \abs{W(t+1)}-\abs{W(t)}
      =\sum_{j=1}^k(\abs{v_j}+\abs{s_j})>0.
  \]
  Thus the words \(W(t)\) have pairwise distinct lengths. They are
  canonical, and injectivity in \textup{(U2)} makes the values \(N(t)\)
  pairwise distinct.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Length-order audit.}
The preceding proof is the only place in the general theorem chain for
recurrent numeration where strict ordering by canonical length was used in the
original argument. Its later appearances were
consequences of the resulting value monotonicity, and are discharged as
follows. In \Cref{thm:mcfl-local-adic-fingerprint}, pairwise distinctness
separates a return point from the original point. In
\Cref{lem:s-unit-increasing-recurrence-rigidity,thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray},
the extracted recurrence needs only pairwise distinct positive terms. In
\Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain}, a sufficiently large multiple
of a return time selects a value larger than the current one. The same
finite-below-current-value argument supplies every increasing choice in
\Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-divisibility-tree}. These exhaust the downstream uses;
the strict increase of the place-value sequence in \textup{(U1)} is a
separate hypothesis and remains in force.

  \label{lem:synchronized-ray-linear-mcfg}
  Fix \(k\ge1\), a word \(a\), and words
  \(u_1,\ldots,u_{k+1},v_1,\ldots,v_k,w_1,\ldots,w_k,

\begin{theorem}[Geometric-ray characterization]
  \label{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}
  For a canonical eventually recurrent numeration system satisfying
  \textup{(U1)}, \textup{(U2)}, and \textup{(U4)}, the following are
  equivalent.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
    \item There are a finite \(k\) and an infinite \(k\)-MCFL
    \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) such that
    \[
      \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(\val_U(w))<\infty.
    \]
    \item The system admits a geometric synchronized scheme in the
    sense of \Cref{def:geometric-synchronized-scheme}.
    \item The language \(\mathcal R_U\) contains an infinite linear MCFL
    \(L_0=\{W(t):t\ge0\}\) of finite fan-out for which there are
    \(c\ge1,b\ge2\) satisfying
    \[
      \val_U(W(t))=cb^t\qquad(t\ge0).
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  Suppose first that \textup{(i)} holds. Use the minimal tail recurrence
  as the witness in
  \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}, and write its resulting
  ray and pairwise distinct value sequence as \(W(t)\) and \(N(t)\).
  Let
  \[
    K_0=\max_{t\ge0}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(N(t)),
  \]
  and choose \(t_0\) attaining the maximum. Let \(T\) be the set of
  primes outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\) that divide \(N(t_0)\), and put
  \(q=\prod_{\ell\in T}\ell\). If \(T\ne\varnothing\), take the return
  time \(H=H(q)\) from
  \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}; if \(T=\varnothing\),
  put \(H=1\). Every prime in \(T\) divides every \(N(t_0+nH)\). A prime
  divisor outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\cup T\) would therefore give at least
  \(K_0+1\) distinct prime divisors outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\), contrary
  to the definition of \(K_0\). Thus all terms of
  \[
    Y(n)=N(t_0+nH)
  \]
  are supported on the fixed finite set \(S_{\mathrm r}\cup T\).

  To make the termwise-product closure explicit, put
  \(n_0=d_{\mathrm r}+1\), list the \(2k\) powered affine blocks as
  \(B_1,\ldots,B_{2k}\), and form
  \[
    K=B_1\otimes\cdots\otimes B_{2k}.
  \]
  Since \(K^t=B_1^t\otimes\cdots\otimes B_{2k}^t\), expansion of the
  interspersed constant block matrices expresses \(N(t)\) as a fixed
  linear functional of \(K^t\). Cayley--Hamilton therefore gives a
  recurrence of order at most
  \[
    R=n_0^{2k}=(d_{\mathrm r}+1)^{2k}.
  \]
  Arithmetic subsequences of a recurrence are recurrences, so \(Y\) is a
  pairwise distinct positive integer recurrence. By
  \Cref{lem:s-unit-increasing-recurrence-rigidity}, there are
  \(r\ge0,h\ge1,c\ge1,b\ge2\) such that
  \(N(t_\ast+h_\ast n)=cb^n\), where
  \(t_\ast=t_0+Hr\) and \(h_\ast=Hh\).

  In the synchronized factorization, replace
  \[
    u_j\ \text{by}\ u_jv_j^{t_\ast},\qquad
    v_j\ \text{by}\ v_j^{h_\ast},\qquad
    w_j\ \text{by}\ w_js_j^{t_\ast},\qquad
    s_j\ \text{by}\ s_j^{h_\ast}.
  \]
  This absorbs the fixed powers and parametrizes exactly the subray
  \(W(t_\ast+h_\ast n)\). Its total pumped length remains positive, so
  it is a geometric synchronized scheme. This proves
  \textup{(i)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(ii)}.

  The implication \textup{(ii)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(iii)} is
  \Cref{lem:synchronized-ray-linear-mcfg}. Finally, under
  \textup{(iii)}, the language \(L_0\) is an infinite MCFL and
  \[
    \omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(cb^t)\le\omega(cb)
    \qquad(t\ge0),
  \]
  proving \textup{(i)}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Prime support of the geometric ratio]
  \label{lem:geometric-ratio-tail-support}
  In every geometric synchronized scheme
  \(\val_U(W(t))=cb^t\), each prime divisor of \(b\) divides the
  constant coefficient \(c_0\) of the minimal tail recurrence.  Equivalently,
  \[
    \operatorname{rad}(b)\mid\operatorname{rad}(\abs{c_0}).
  \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
  Suppose that a prime \(p\mid b\) does not divide \(c_0\), put
  \(e=v_p(c)\), and take the allowed modulus \(q=p^{e+1}\).  Every
  nonempty block matrix among the \(M_{v_j}\) and \(M_{s_j}\) is invertible
  modulo \(q\) by \Cref{lem:affine-recurrence-block-action}.  A common
  multiple \(H\ge1\) of their orders gives, by the matrix product defining
  the scheme exactly as in the proof of
  \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit},
  \[
    \val_U(W(t+H))\equiv\val_U(W(t))\pmod q
    \qquad(t\ge0).
  \]
  At \(t=0\) this says
  \[
    cb^H\equiv c\pmod {p^{e+1}}.
  \]
  But \(p\mid b\) implies \(p\nmid b^H-1\), so
  \(v_p(c(b^H-1))=e\), contradicting the displayed congruence.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Positive semidecidability on promised presentations]
  \label{cor:bounded-outside-support-semidecidable}
  On the promised class of valid presentations satisfying
  \textup{(U1)}, \textup{(U2)}, and \textup{(U4)}, suppose the finite
  digit alphabet, recurrence and initial data, and a DFA recognizing
  \(\mathcal R_U\) are supplied,
  together with a supplied or effectively certified minimal tail
  recurrence and a valid threshold \(J_{\mathrm r}\). Then the set of
  positive promised instances of the property in
  \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}\textup{(i)} is
  recursively enumerable, equivalently it has a \(\Sigma^0_1\) upper
  bound. No recognition procedure for membership in the promised input
  class is asserted.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
  Enumerate \(k\ge1\), \(a\in A^{J_{\mathrm r}}\), and all finite tuples
  of words occurring in
  \Cref{def:geometric-synchronized-scheme}, rejecting tuples of zero
  total pumped length. For a fixed tuple, whether the DFA accepts
  \(W(t)\) for every \(t\ge0\) is decidable: the tuple of powers of the
  finitely many pumped-block transformations is eventually periodic in
  the finite transition monoid, and its preperiod and period are found
  by exhaustive iteration.

  The affine matrices construct an exact linear recurrence for
  \[
    N(t)=\val_U(W(t)).
  \]
  With \(d_{\mathrm r}\) the minimal tail order, the Kronecker construction
  in the proof of
  \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray} has dimension
  \[
    R=(d_{\mathrm r}+1)^{2k};
  \]
  it is computable from the candidate and is an upper bound for the
  recurrence order of \(N(t)\). For a tuple accepted at every parameter,
  compute \(c=N(0)\). The only
  possible integer ratio is \(b=N(1)/N(0)\). Check that
  \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\), and then decide whether the recurrence
  \(N(t+1)-bN(t)\) is identically zero by checking its first \(R\) terms;
  Cayley--Hamilton makes those \(R\) zero values sufficient. Thus each
  candidate scheme is decidable, and the enumeration halts exactly on
  positive promised instances by
  \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}. No claim of a
  decision procedure for negative instances is made.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Exact algorithmic boundary]
  \label{rem:general-decision-interface}
  The preceding corollary does not yield a decision procedure. To turn
  its enumeration into one, it would suffice to compute from the input
  DFA and minimal tail recurrence a bound \(B\) such that every positive
  instance has a geometric synchronized scheme with fan-out and total
  constant and pumped-block length at most \(B\). No such compression
  follows from DFA pumping: replacing a long loop by a shorter word with
  the same DFA endpoints need not preserve its affine recurrence matrix,
  and can therefore destroy the identity
  \(\val_U(W(t+1))=b\val_U(W(t))\).

  The neighboring decision theory does not close this step. Skolem asks
  whether one term of a recurrence vanishes, while Positivity and Ultimate
  Positivity ask for signs of all or all sufficiently late terms; these
  problems remain open in unrestricted order
  \cite{OuaknineWorrell2012,AkshayBazilleGenestVahanwala2024}.
  Tarasov--Vyalyi relate an orbit-hitting problem to regular-language
  intersection \cite{TarasovVyalyi2011}, while unrestricted multiplicative
  matrix equations include undecidable families
  \cite{BellEtAl2008MatrixEquations}. Our candidate check instead asks
  whether the explicitly constructed recurrence
  \(N(t+1)-bN(t)\) is identically zero; no reduction in either direction is
  claimed. None of these observations is a reduction for the companion-form
  digit matrices here, and conditions
  \textup{(U1)}, \textup{(U2)}, and \textup{(U4)} must also be preserved.
  Thus general decidability,
  undecidability, and any hardness classification remain open; the proved
  effective statement is exactly the positive semidecision above. The
  weak-Perron subclass of greedy linear numeration bases is resolved
  separately below.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Arbitrarily deep quotient congruences]
  \label{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain}
  Suppose \(\abs{a_0}=1\), and let \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) be an
  infinite MCFL. For arbitrary sequences \(M_i\ge1\) and \(r_i\ge1\),
  \(L\) contains a strictly increasing sequence \(N_i\) such that
  \[
    N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i,\qquad Q_i>1,\qquad
    Q_i\equiv1\pmod {M_iN_i^{r_i}}.
  \]
  If \(M_i\) is divisible by every prime at most \(B_i\), then every
  prime divisor of \(Q_i\) exceeds \(B_i\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  Take the fixed orbit \(N(t)\) from
  \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}, discarding finitely many
  initial parameters so that \(N(t)\ge2\). Having selected
  \(N_i=N(t_i)\), apply the synchronized congruence with
  \[
    q_i=M_iN_i^{r_i+1}.
  \]
  The values \(N(t_i+mH(q_i))\), \(m\ge1\), are pairwise distinct and all
  are congruent to \(N_i\) modulo \(q_i\). Only finitely many positive
  integers are at most \(N_i\), so choose \(m_i\ge1\) for which
  \(N(t_i+m_iH(q_i))>N_i\), and set
  \(t_{i+1}=t_i+m_iH(q_i)\). The congruence gives
  \[
    N_{i+1}=N_i+c_iM_iN_i^{r_i+1}
           =N_i(1+c_iM_iN_i^{r_i})
  \]
  for an integer \(c_i\ge1\). This proves the first assertion. Under
  the last hypothesis, \(Q_i\equiv1\pmod p\) for every prime
  \(p\le B_i\), so none of those primes divides \(Q_i\).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Induced full divisibility tree]
  \label{thm:unit-mcfl-divisibility-tree}
  Under the hypotheses of
  \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain}, there is an injection
  \[
    \Phi:\NN^{<\omega}\longrightarrow L
  \]
  such that
  \[
    \val_U(\Phi(\sigma))\mid\val_U(\Phi(\tau))
      \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma\preceq\tau,
  \]
  where \(\preceq\) denotes the prefix order. The quotients attached to
  distinct edges can be chosen pairwise coprime. Moreover, given an
  arbitrary prescribed threshold for each edge, every prime divisor of
  its quotient can be required to exceed that threshold.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  Use the fixed pairwise-distinct orbit from
  \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}. Here is an explicit
  parent-before-child enumeration. If \(p_i\) is the \(i\)-th prime, encode
  \(\sigma=(\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_{m-1})\) by
  \[
    \kappa(\sigma)=2^m\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}p_{i+2}^{\sigma_i+1}.
  \]
  Unique factorization makes \(\kappa\) injective, and
  \(\kappa(\sigma^\frown j)>\kappa(\sigma)\). Enumerating the nonroot
  nodes, equivalently their incoming edges, by increasing \(\kappa\)
  therefore has order type \(\omega\) and places every parent before each
  child. Map
  the root to any orbit word of value \(R_0\ge2\). Suppose finitely many
  edges have been assigned, and consider a new edge from a parent of
  value \(P\). Let \(R\) be divisible by \(R_0\), by every previously
  assigned edge quotient, and by every prime not exceeding the prescribed
  threshold for the new edge. Apply the synchronized orbit congruence
  modulo \(P^2R\) at the parameter of the parent. Positive multiples of
  the return time give pairwise distinct positive values in the indicated
  congruence class. Only finitely many are at most \(P\), so some multiple
  gives an unused orbit word of value \(P'>P\) with
  \[
    P'\equiv P\pmod {P^2R}.
  \]
  Hence \(P'=PQ\), where \(Q>1\) and \(Q\equiv1\pmod {PR}\). In
  particular, \(Q\) is coprime to the root and to every earlier edge
  quotient, and no prime up to the prescribed threshold divides \(Q\).

  Recursion defines \(\Phi\) on every node. The value at a node is the
  root value times the product of the edge quotients along its path.
  Since the root and all distinct edge quotients are pairwise coprime,
  the value at \(\sigma\) divides the value at \(\tau\) exactly when the
  root-to-\(\sigma\) edge set is contained in the root-to-\(\tau\) edge
  set. For two nodes of a rooted tree, containment of their root-path edge
  sets holds exactly when the first node is an ancestor of the second;
  here this is precisely \(\sigma\preceq\tau\). This also proves injectivity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Prime immunity for recurrent numeration systems]
  \label{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity}
  Let \((U,A,\mathcal R_U)\) satisfy \textup{(U1)}, \textup{(U2)}, and
  \textup{(U4)}, and put
  \[
    \mathcal P_U
      :=\{w\in\mathcal R_U:\val_U(w)\text{ is prime}\}.
  \]
  Then \(\mathcal P_U\) is MCF-immune, and therefore CF-immune,
  REG-immune, and not recognizable by a finite automaton over \(A\).

  If, in addition, \(\abs{a_0}=1\), then every infinite multiple
  context-free
  \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) has unbounded
  \(\omega(\val_U(w))\). More precisely, \(L\) contains a
  coprime-quotient chain \(N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i\) with
  \(Q_i>1\) and \(Q_i\equiv1\pmod {N_i}\). Thus the bounded-\(\omega\),
  bounded-\(\Omega\), and finite-prime-support languages of a unit
  system are MCF-immune whenever they are infinite. Without the unit
  hypothesis, every bounded-\(\Omega\) language is still MCF-immune.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  The MCF-immunity assertions follow from
  \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}, including its
  bounded-\(\Omega\) conclusion. In a unit system \(S\) is empty, so
  that theorem gives unbounded \(\omega\). Taking
  \(M_i=r_i=1\) in
  \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} gives the stated chain.
  Regular languages are context-free and context-free languages are
  MCFLs. Finally, \textup{(U2)} and Euclid's theorem make
  \(\mathcal P_U\) infinite.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Greedy length interval.}
For a standard greedy linear numeration basis with \(U_0=1\), a positive
integer has a canonical greedy word of length \(m\) if and only if it lies
in the half-open interval
\[
  [U_{m-1},U_m).
\]
Indeed, the greedy algorithm chooses the least threshold \(U_m\) strictly
larger than the represented integer; minimality of \(m\) gives the lower
bound, and the choice of \(U_m\) gives the upper bound. This is a property
of the standard greedy subclass, not an assumption on the ambient
canonical eventually recurrent systems.

\begin{corollary}[Linear numeration bases with Perron recurrence]
  \label{cor:linear-perron-prime-cf-immunity}
  Let \(U=(U_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a standard greedy linear numeration basis in
  the following precise sense: \(U_0=1\), the \(U_n\) are strictly
  increasing integers with bounded quotients, \(\mathcal R_U\) is the LSD-first
  reversal of the usual greedy representation language, and \(U\)
  has minimal tail recurrence polynomial equal to the minimal polynomial
  of a Perron number \(\beta\). Thus
  \(\beta>1\) is a real algebraic integer and every other conjugate
  \(\beta'\) satisfies \(\abs{\beta'}<\beta\); compare
  \cite{LindMarcus1995,Rigo2014Vol2}. Then its prime
  representation language is MCF-immune, hence CF-immune, REG-immune and
  nonrecognizable. The same statements hold in the usual MSD-first
  convention.

  If the dominant Perron number is a unit and the chosen recurrence has
  trailing coefficient \(a_0=\pm1\), then the full coprime-quotient and
  bounded-prime-support MCF-immunity conclusions of
  \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity} hold.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
  Greedy expansion gives a unique representation of every positive
  integer, and its length-\(m\) words represent values between successive
  place-value thresholds; thus \textup{(U1)} and \textup{(U2)} hold. The defining
  Perron recurrence gives \textup{(U4)}. Apply
  \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity}. The immunity proof
  uses only \textup{(U1)}, \textup{(U2)}, and \textup{(U4)} and does not
  assume that the full greedy language is regular. In the Pisot subclass,
  Frougny's finite
  normalization theorem supplies a finite transducer, and the associated
  canonical syntax and Bertrand/substitution descriptions are standard
  \cite{Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,Fabre1995,FrougnySolomyak1992}.
  Finally, multiple context-free, context-free, and
  regular languages are closed under reversal, so changing between the LSD-first proof
  convention and the usual MSD-first convention preserves every
  conclusion.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Pisot and non-Pisot Perron systems]
  \label{ex:pisot-unit-nonunit}
  The Fibonacci recurrence has characteristic polynomial
  \(X^2-X-1\), the Pell recurrence has \(X^2-2X-1\), and the
  Tribonacci recurrence has \(X^3-X^2-X-1\). Their trailing recurrence
  coefficient is \(a_0=1\), so the iterated conclusion applies. In
  ordinary base \(b\), \(U_n=b^n\) and \(a_0=b\); prime MCF-immunity
  follows, strengthening the classical fixed-base CF-immunity conclusion
  to MCF-immunity, but the unit iteration is not being asserted.

  There is also an infinite family of genuinely nonintegral weak-Perron
  systems. Let \(p,q\ge2\), put \(B=pq\), and suppose that \(B\) is not a
  square. Define
  \[
    U_{2t}=B^t,\qquad U_{2t+1}=pB^t\qquad(t\ge0).
  \]
  The successive quotients are alternately \(p\) and \(q\). Repeated
  Euclidean division in these alternating radices gives every positive
  integer a unique greedy expansion: the digit at an even position lies
  in \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\), and the digit at an odd position lies in
  \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\). Hence the LSD-first canonical language is regular,
  since a finite automaton need only track position parity, the relevant
  digit bound, and a nonzero final digit. Moreover,
  \[
    U_{n+2}=BU_n,
  \]
  and the irreducible polynomial \(X^2-B\) is the minimal recurrence
  polynomial. Its positive root \(\sqrt B\) is nonintegral and weak Perron,
  with conjugate \(-\sqrt B\) of the same modulus. The regular ray
  \(\{0^{2t}1:t\ge0\}\) has values \(B^t\). Thus \(p=2,q=3\) gives the
  sequence \(1,2,6,12,36,72,\ldots\), while \(p=2,q=5\) gives a second
  concrete member \(1,2,10,20,100,200,\ldots\).

  A genuinely nonintegral, nonunit Pisot example is obtained from
  \[
    U_0=1,\qquad U_1=3,\qquad
    U_{n+2}=2U_{n+1}+2U_n.
  \]
  If \(2<U_{n+1}/U_n\le3\), then
  \[
    \frac{U_{n+2}}{U_{n+1}}
      =2+\frac{2U_n}{U_{n+1}}\in[8/3,3),
  \]
  so induction from \(U_1/U_0=3\) proves strict increase and bounded
  quotients. The irreducible polynomial \(X^2-2X-2\) annihilates this
  nonzero rational sequence, hence is its minimal tail polynomial. Its
  dominant root is \(1+\sqrt3\), and its trailing coefficient is
  \(a_0=2\), so the action is singular modulo \(2\). Nevertheless,
  \Cref{cor:linear-perron-bounded-support-classification} shows that every
  infinite MCFL in this nonintegral system acquires unbounded prime support
  away from \(2\); singularity of the ambient action does not produce a
  valuation-only escape language.

  The polynomial \(X^2-5X+5\) gives a genuinely non-Pisot instance. Its
  dominant root \(\beta=(5+\sqrt5)/2\) is Perron, while its other conjugate
  \((5-\sqrt5)/2\) is greater than one. The integer sequence
  \[
    U_0=1,\qquad U_1=4,\qquad
    U_{n+2}=5U_{n+1}-5U_n
  \]
  begins \(1,4,15,55,200,\ldots\) and is strictly increasing. Indeed,
  \[
    U_{n+1}>3U_n>0
  \]
  holds at \(n=0\), and if it holds at \(n\), then
  \[
    U_{n+2}=5(U_{n+1}-U_n)
      >\frac{10}{3}U_{n+1}>3U_{n+1}.
  \]
  Moreover, if \(3<U_{n+1}/U_n\le4\), then
  \[
    \frac{U_{n+2}}{U_{n+1}}
      =5-\frac{5U_n}{U_{n+1}}
      \le 5-\frac54<4,
  \]
  while the lower bound was just proved; starting from \(U_1/U_0=4\)
  therefore gives \(3<U_{n+1}/U_n\le4\) for every \(n\). Thus the quotients
  are bounded, so its greedy language is the greedy language of a linear
  numeration basis with Perron recurrence in the stated sense. The
  classification below implies that every infinite MCFL in this standard
  greedy language has unbounded prime support away from \(5\).
\end{example}

\begin{theorem}[Weak-Perron radical classification]
  \label{cor:linear-perron-bounded-support-classification}
  Let \(U=(U_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a standard greedy linear numeration basis with
  \(U_0=1\), strictly increasing integer place values with bounded
  quotients, and let \(\mathcal R_U\) be the LSD-first reversal of its
  greedy representation language. Suppose that the minimal tail recurrence
  polynomial \(\mu_U\) is the minimal polynomial of a weak Perron number
  \(\beta>1\), meaning that every conjugate \(\beta'\) satisfies
  \(\abs{\beta'}\le\beta\). Let \(S_{\mathrm r}\) be the set of prime
  divisors of \(\mu_U(0)\). The residue-growth step below is a
  coefficient-level specialization of the quotient-limit mechanism in
  \cite[Proposition~10 and Remark~12]{CharlierKreczman2025}; the
  prime-support/MCFL equivalence is not contained there. With this
  attribution understood, the following are equivalent:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
    \item There exist \(k<\infty\) and an infinite \(k\)-MCFL
    \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) such that
    \[
      \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(\val_U(w))<\infty;
    \]
    \item \(\mathcal R_U\) contains a geometric synchronized scheme whose
    values are \(cb^t\), with \(c\ge1\), \(b\ge2\);
    \item Some positive power of \(\beta\) is an integer:
    \[
      \beta^m=B\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}
      \quad\text{for some }m\ge1;
    \]
    \item For some \(m\ge1\) and \(B\ge2\),
    \[
      \mu_U(X)\mid X^m-B;
    \]
    \item For some \(m\ge1\), \(B\ge2\), and \(n_0\),
    \[
      U_{n+m}=BU_n\qquad(n\ge n_0).
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
  In the positive case, \(\mathcal R_U\) already contains the infinite
  regular ray
  \[
    \{0^{n_0+mt}1:t\ge0\},\qquad
    \val_U(0^{n_0+mt}1)=U_{n_0}B^t.
  \]
  Consequently, if no positive power of \(\beta\) is an integer, then every
  infinite MCFL \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) has
  \[
    \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(\val_U(w))=\infty.
  \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  The equivalence of \textup{(i)} and \textup{(ii)} is
  \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}.

  \input{sec_pisot_weak_perron_analysis}

  Suppose now that \textup{(ii)} holds, and write
  \[
    \val_U(W(t))=cb^t,
    \qquad \abs{W(t)}=L+Dt,
  \]
  where \(D>0\) is the total pumped length.  In a greedy \(U\)-system, a
  canonical word of length \(m\) represents a value in the half-open interval
  \([U_{m-1},U_m)\).  Hence
  \[
    U_{L+Dt-1}\le cb^t<U_{L+Dt}.
  \]
  For \(k_t=L+Dt\), the root limit gives
  \[
    U_{k_t}^{1/t}
      =\left(U_{k_t}^{1/k_t}\right)^{k_t/t}\longrightarrow\beta^D,
    \qquad
    U_{k_t-1}^{1/t}
      =\left(U_{k_t-1}^{1/(k_t-1)}\right)^{(k_t-1)/t}
       \longrightarrow\beta^D.
  \]
  Since \((cb^t)^{1/t}\to b\), taking \(t\)-th roots in the preceding
  squeeze yields \(b=\beta^D\). This is \textup{(iii)} with \(m=D\) and
  \(B=b\).

  Conditions \textup{(iii)} and \textup{(iv)} are equivalent because
  \(\beta^m=B\) says exactly that the minimal polynomial \(\mu_U\) of
  \(\beta\) divides \(X^m-B\) in \(\mathbb Q[X]\). Conditions
  \textup{(iv)} and \textup{(v)} are equivalent by the definition of
  \(\mu_U\) as the monic generator of \(I_U^{\mathrm{tail}}\): the
  divisibility \(\mu_U\mid X^m-B\) puts \(X^m-B\) in that ideal and gives
  \(U_{n+m}=BU_n\) eventually, while an eventual identity of this form
  puts \(X^m-B\) in the ideal and hence forces the divisibility.

  Finally, assume \textup{(v)} and enlarge \(n_0\), if necessary, so that
  \(n_0\ge J_{\mathrm r}\). The greedy representation of \(U_n\), in the
  LSD-first convention, is \(0^n1\). Taking
  \[
    a=0^{J_{\mathrm r}},\quad k=1,\quad
    u_1=0^{n_0-J_{\mathrm r}},\quad v_1=0^m,\quad
    w_1=s_1=\varepsilon,\quad u_2=1
  \]
  gives canonical words \(W(t)=0^{n_0+mt}1\) and
  \[
    \val_U(W(t))=U_{n_0}B^t.
  \]
  This is the asserted regular geometric ray and proves
  \textup{(v)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(ii)}. The final assertion is the
  negation of \textup{(i)}. In the strict-Perron subclass, the equality
  \(b=\beta^D\) forces every conjugate to have modulus \(\beta\) unless
  \(\beta\) has degree one; hence the theorem recovers the previous
  integral-root boundary there.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Exact open interfaces]
  \label{rem:pisot-open-interfaces}
  The terminology for linear numeration systems with Perron or Pisot
  recurrence is not uniform.
  \Cref{cor:linear-perron-prime-cf-immunity} covers the standard
  positional linear \(U\)-systems just specified, including integer
  bases, Zeckendorf/Fibonacci, Pell, higher-order Pisot recurrences, and
  non-Pisot Perron examples such as \(X^2-5X+5\).
  It asserts nothing about R\'enyi \(\beta\)-expansions, \(\beta\)-shifts,
  Parry languages, \(\beta\)-integers, Cantor real bases, or abstract
  numeration systems. Real-base systems do not in general provide the
  bijective finite-word-to-\(\mathbb N\) positional map and integral affine
  block action used here; \(\beta\)-shifts and Parry languages encode a
  dynamical admissibility problem rather than this integer-valued affine
  recurrence. Cantor real bases have nonstationary real place weights, while
  abstract numeration assigns genealogical ranks rather than values of the
  form \(\sum_j a_jU_j\). Redundant noninjective digit systems and systems
  without an eventual integral recurrence are likewise outside the stated
  hypotheses. Consequently no transfer to any of these settings is claimed.

  For a fixed nonunit recurrence witness, the ambient action can be
  singular modulo primes dividing \(a_0\), so the unrestricted unit-system
  divisibility tree need not follow. The witness-relative surviving
  statement is \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}: every infinite
  MCFL must acquire unbounded prime support outside that finite set or
  unbounded valuation at one of its primes. The invariant restricted
  action and the failure of arbitrary recurrence witnesses to classify
  escape behavior are distinguished in
  \Cref{prop:recurrence-witness-separation}.
  Within greedy linear numeration bases with weak-Perron recurrence, the
  residual alternative is classified by
  \Cref{cor:linear-perron-bounded-support-classification}: it occurs exactly
  when a positive power of the weak Perron number is an integer. The
  ordinary-base example preceding
  \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} shows that the valuation
  alternative cannot be removed.
\end{remark}

\section{A slender-context-free two-system theorem}
\label{sec:slender-cobham}

This section has a different architecture from the preceding one-system
MCFL argument. It uses a global finite cover of each full representation
language, turns every member of that cover into finitely many recurrence
sequences, and invokes finiteness of common values. In particular, none of
the finite-group return, deleted-prime, fixed-support quotient,
geometric-subsequence, or divisibility-tree arguments enters the proof.

We record the two external inputs with their hypotheses. A language \(L\)
is \emph{slender} when
\(\sup_n\#(L\cap A^n)<\infty\). In the terminology of
Ilie--Rozenberg--Salomaa, this is \(0\)-poly-slender, and a \(1\)-Dyck loop
is a language
\[
  \{u v^n w x^n y:n\ge0\}.
\]
Their Theorem~7 states that a context-free language is \(0\)-poly-slender
if and only if it is a finite union of \(1\)-Dyck loops
\cite[Theorem~7]{IlieRozenbergSalomaa2000}. The characterization was first
proved, in the equivalent terminology of iterative or semidiscrete
context-free languages, by Latteux--Thierrin
\cite{LatteuxThierrin1983}, and independently by Ilie
\cite{Ilie1994}.

Mignotte's common-value theorem concerns two rational-integer linear
recurrence sequences. We use the following precise dominant-root form. The
input consists of ordinary recurrences indexed from (0), together with
expansions
\[
  A_n=a\lambda^n+\sum_{i=2}^s P_i(n)\lambda_i^n,
  \qquad
  B_m=b\kappa^m+\sum_{j=2}^t Q_j(m)\kappa_j^m,
\]
where \(a,b\ne0\), the characteristic roots and coefficients are
algebraic, \(\lambda,\kappa>1\), and
\(
  \abs{\lambda_i}<\lambda,
  \abs{\kappa_j}<\kappa
\)
for all remaining characteristic roots. If \(\lambda\) and \(\kappa\)
are multiplicatively independent, Mignotte's proof effectively produces an
integer \(M(A,B)\) such that
\begin{equation}
  A_n=B_m,\quad n\ge M(A,B)
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  a\lambda^n=b\kappa^m.
  \label{eq:mignotte-effective-threshold}
\end{equation}
The same assertion with the sequences interchanged produces \(M(B,A)\).
In particular \(A_n=B_m\) has only finitely many nonnegative integer
solutions \cite{Mignotte1978Intersection}; Bennett--Pint\'er give an
accessible published restatement of the integral-recurrence,
unique-dominant-root hypotheses \cite{BennettPinter2015}. The qualitative
theorem below uses only finiteness. The effective refinement retains the two
thresholds in \eqref{eq:mignotte-effective-threshold}.

The next lemma supplies the hypothesis that is not a consequence merely of
the root-growth squeeze.

\begin{lemma}[Dominant-root transfer for a paired greedy loop]
  \label{lem:paired-loop-dominant-root-transfer}
  Let \(U=(U_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a strictly increasing standard greedy linear
  numeration sequence. Suppose that its least eventual recurrence
  polynomial is the minimal polynomial \(\mu\) of a weak Perron number
  \(\alpha>1\). If
  \[
    z_n=u v^n w x^n y\in\mathcal R_U\qquad(n\ge0)
  \]
  and \(D=\abs v+\abs x>0\), then there is \(h\ge1\) such that, for every
  \(0\le r<h\), the integer sequence
  \[
    Z_r(t)=\val_U(z_{ht+r})\qquad(t\ge0)
  \]
  is eventually a linear recurrence whose least eventual characteristic
  roots have the unique dominating root
  \[
    \alpha^{hD}.
  \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
  We audit the actual affine matrices. Let \(C\) be the companion matrix of
  \(\mu\). For a block \(b=b_1\cdots b_\ell\), multiplication of the digit
  matrices in \Cref{lem:affine-recurrence-block-action} gives
  \begin{equation}
    M_b=
    \begin{pmatrix}1&q_b\\0&C^\ell\end{pmatrix}
    \label{eq:paired-loop-affine-block-form}
  \end{equation}
  for a row \(q_b\), with \(M_\varepsilon=I\). Because \(\mu\) is
  irreducible over characteristic zero, it is separable, so \(C\) is
  diagonalizable over a splitting field. Hence \(C^\ell\) is
  diagonalizable even when distinct conjugates acquire the same
  \(\ell\)-th power. The eigenvalues of \(M_b\) are \(1\) and
  \(\gamma^\ell\), where \(\gamma\) runs over the conjugates of \(\alpha\).
  If \(b\ne\varepsilon\), every peripheral eigenvalue has modulus
  \(\alpha^\ell>1\), so it cannot collide with the affine eigenvalue \(1\).
  Equation \eqref{eq:paired-loop-affine-block-form} then shows that its
  peripheral generalized eigenspace is semisimple. Thus the affine row
  creates neither a peripheral eigenvalue nor a peripheral Jordan block.

  Discarding finitely many initial parameters puts the reading position
  beyond the recurrence transient. If \(v\ne\varepsilon\), the represented
  value is then a fixed scalar functional of
  \[
    M_x^n A M_v^n
  \]
  for one fixed matrix \(A\); if \(v=\varepsilon\), it is a fixed scalar
  functional of \(M_x^n A\). This follows directly by reading the five
  fixed blocks in LSD-first order; fixed initial powers used to cross the
  transient are absorbed into \(A\). Vectorization in the first case gives
  the actual powering matrix
  \[
    K=M_v^{\mathsf T}\otimes M_x,
  \]
  with the evident one-factor interpretation when one pumped block is
  empty. Its spectral radius is \(\alpha^D\). Its peripheral eigenvalues
  are exactly the products
  \(
    \gamma_1^{\abs v}\gamma_2^{\abs x}
  \)
  obtained from peripheral conjugates in the nonempty factors, and their
  generalized eigenspaces are semisimple by the preceding paragraph and
  the tensor-product Jordan formula.

  Choose \(h\) from the weak-Perron power characterization, so that
  \[
    \abs\gamma=\alpha\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    \gamma^h=\alpha^h
  \]
  for every conjugate \(\gamma\). Every peripheral eigenvalue of \(K^h\) is then
  the same positive number
  \(
    \Lambda=\alpha^{hD}
  \), and the \(\Lambda\)-generalized eigenspace is still semisimple.
  All other eigenvalues of \(K^h\) have modulus strictly below
  \(\Lambda\). Cayley--Hamilton applied to the displayed scalar functional
  therefore gives, for each residue \(r\),
  \begin{equation}
    Z_r(t)=c_r\Lambda^t+
      \sum_j P_{r,j}(t)\xi_{r,j}^t,
    \qquad \abs{\xi_{r,j}}<\Lambda.
    \label{eq:paired-loop-spectral-expansion}
  \end{equation}
  This proves at matrix level that peripheral collisions coalesce to one
  algebraic root and that no polynomial factor in \(t\) can accompany it.

  It remains to audit cancellation by the actual value functional. The
  word \(z_{ht+r}\) has length \(L_r+hDt\) for a fixed \(L_r\). Greedy
  validity gives
  \[
    U_{L_r+hDt-1}\le Z_r(t)<U_{L_r+hDt}.
  \]
  The positive residue asymptotics
  \eqref{eq:weak-perron-residue-asymptotic}--
  \eqref{eq:weak-perron-positive-residues}, applied to these two fixed
  index residues for the chosen period, show
  \[
    0<\liminf_{t\to\infty}\frac{Z_r(t)}{\Lambda^t}
      \le
      \limsup_{t\to\infty}\frac{Z_r(t)}{\Lambda^t}<\infty.
  \]
  In \eqref{eq:paired-loop-spectral-expansion} every lower-modulus term,
  including all its possible Jordan polynomials, is \(o(\Lambda^t)\).
  Consequently the spectral-projection coefficient \(c_r\) of the actual
  affine value functional is nonzero (indeed positive). Total peripheral
  cancellation is therefore impossible, and \(\Lambda\) survives as the
  unique dominating root of the least scalar recurrence.
\end{proof}

For \(X\subseteq\NN_{\ge1}\), write
\[
  \operatorname{Rep}_U(X)
    =\{z\in\mathcal R_U:\val_U(z)\in X\}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Slender-context-free Cobham theorem]
  \label{thm:slender-cfl-cobham}
  Let \(U\) and \(V\) be strictly increasing standard greedy linear
  numeration sequences whose least eventual recurrence polynomials are the
  minimal polynomials of weak Perron numbers \(\alpha>1\) and \(\beta>1\),
  respectively. Suppose that \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are multiplicatively
  independent. If, for one set \(X\subseteq\NN_{\ge1}\), both full
  representation languages
  \[
    \operatorname{Rep}_U(X)
    \quad\hbox{and}\quad
    \operatorname{Rep}_V(X)
  \]
  are slender context-free languages, then \(X\) is finite.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  Suppose that \(X\) is infinite. The paired-loop classification gives
  finite covers
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \operatorname{Rep}_U(X)
        &=\bigcup_{i=1}^a
          \{u_i v_i^n w_i x_i^n y_i:n\ge0\},\\
      \operatorname{Rep}_V(X)
        &=\bigcup_{j=1}^b
          \{u'_j(v'_j)^m w'_j(x'_j)^m y'_j:m\ge0\}.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  Loops with zero total pumped length are singletons and may be removed;
  they cover only finitely many values. Apply
  \Cref{lem:paired-loop-dominant-root-transfer} to every remaining loop.
  After the finitely many residue restrictions, \(X\) is covered in each
  system by finitely many integer recurrence sequences having respective
  unique dominating roots
  \[
    \alpha^{h_i(\abs{v_i}+\abs{x_i})}
    \quad\hbox{and}\quad
    \beta^{k_j(\abs{v'_j}+\abs{x'_j})}.
  \]
  Infinitely many elements of \(X\) must lie in the intersection of the
  images of one sequence from the first finite family and one from the
  second. Their dominating roots are multiplicatively independent, since
  they are positive powers of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Mignotte's theorem
  says that the equality of their terms has only finitely many index pairs,
  a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Effective refinement}

We now retain the finite data suppressed in the preceding proof. This is an
effectivity statement from complete presentations, not a uniform estimate in
a few size parameters.

\begin{definition}[Effective two-system presentation]
  \label{def:effective-two-system-presentation}
  An \emph{effective two-system presentation} consists of the following
  finite data, subject to the hypotheses of
  \Cref{thm:slender-cfl-cobham}.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
    \item For each of \(U\) and \(V\), it gives the digit alphabet, the
      initial values, integer recurrence coefficients, and an individual
      valid recurrence threshold. It also gives the least eventual
      polynomial, its distinguished real root by an isolating interval, and
      the certificate that this polynomial is the minimal polynomial of the
      relevant weak Perron number.
    \item For each full representation language it gives either a
      context-free grammar, promised to generate that slender language, or
      an exact finite cover by words
      \(
        u v^n w x^n y
      \)
      with \(n\ge0\). In the grammar case, the constructive form of the
      slender-language theorem computes such a cover from the grammar
      \cite{LatteuxThierrin1983,Ilie1994}; the resulting paired-loop form is
      the one recorded in \cite[Theorem~7]{IlieRozenbergSalomaa2000}.
  \end{enumerate}
  The promises include validity and uniqueness of the represented words and
  exact equality with \(\operatorname{Rep}_U(X)\) and
  \(\operatorname{Rep}_V(X)\). Algebraic numbers are represented by their
  minimal polynomials and isolating data. Thus exact arithmetic, comparison
  of algebraic moduli, and root-of-unity tests are effective.
\end{definition}

The recurrence threshold in (i) belongs to that one presentation; no common
threshold for the two systems, or for different paired loops, is assumed.
Likewise, in (ii) a grammar is a promised input. The assertion is not that an
arbitrary grammar can first be recognized as slender without using that
promise.

\begin{lemma}[Effective dominant-root transfer]
  \label{lem:effective-paired-loop-transfer}
  From the effective recurrence data for \(U\) and one nonconstant valid
  paired loop
  \[
    z_n=u v^n w x^n y,\qquad D=\abs v+\abs x>0,
  \]
  one can compute an integer \(h\ge1\) and, for every \(0\le r<h\), the
  following finite package:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
    \item an individual shift \(s_r\ge0\);
    \item integer recurrence coefficients and enough integer initial values
      to define, from index \(0\), the sequence
      \[
        A_r(t)=\val_U(z_{h(t+s_r)+r})\qquad(t\ge0);
      \]
    \item its unique positive dominant root
      \(\Lambda=\alpha^{hD}\), its algebraic dominant coefficient
      \(c_r>0\), and computable algebraic numbers
      \(C_r>0\) and \(1\le\rho_r<\Lambda\) such that
      \begin{equation}
        \abs{A_r(t)-c_r\Lambda^t}\le C_r\rho_r^t
        \qquad(t\ge0).
        \label{eq:effective-loop-error}
      \end{equation}
  \end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
  All constructions occur in a computable number field containing the roots
  of the supplied minimal polynomial. Compute its conjugates on the circle
  of radius \(\alpha\), test the quotients of peripheral conjugates for being
  roots of unity, and take for \(h\) a common multiple of their orders. This
  is the effective version of the power choice in
  \Cref{lem:paired-loop-dominant-root-transfer}.

  The supplied recurrence threshold is now handled separately for this
  loop. If \(v\ne\varepsilon\), compute how many initial copies of \(v\) are
  needed for the remaining repeated action to start in the stationary
  recurrence range and absorb those copies into the fixed prefix. If
  \(v=\varepsilon\), then \(x\ne\varepsilon\), and do the same with the
  first copies of \(x\). For each residue \(r\), increase the parameter to
  the least resulting value congruent to \(r\pmod h\); this gives the
  recorded, loop- and residue-dependent shift \(s_r\). Every excluded
  parameter is thereby explicit and finite.

  Form the integral affine block matrices from
  \eqref{eq:paired-loop-affine-block-form} and the actual powering matrix
  \(M_v^{\mathsf T}\otimes M_x\), with the one-factor version when a pumped
  block is empty. Applying Cayley--Hamilton to the scalar value functional
  gives integer recurrence coefficients and a computable order; direct
  evaluation gives that many initial values. Exact spectral decomposition
  of its \(h\)-th power gives the coefficient \(c_r\) and all remaining
  algebraic roots and Jordan polynomials. The proof of
  \Cref{lem:paired-loop-dominant-root-transfer} shows that \(c_r\ne0\): the
  greedy length squeeze uses the supplied recurrence threshold and the two
  fixed index residues belonging to this particular loop. Since the values
  are positive, the coefficient is positive.

  Finally compute a real algebraic \(\rho_r\) strictly between the largest
  modulus of a remaining root and \(\Lambda\). The coefficients and degrees
  of the finitely many Jordan polynomials are explicit. Bounding
  \(t^e q^t\) for each \(q<1\), and enlarging the constant to cover the
  finitely many small indices, effectively produces \(C_r\) in
  \eqref{eq:effective-loop-error}. Thus the output is an ordinary recurrence
  beginning at \(0\), not an eventual recurrence with an unrecorded prefix.
\end{proof}

For the next statement, apply the lemma to all nonconstant loops. Index the
resulting recurrence sequences by finite sets \(P\) and \(Q\): write
\[
  A_p(t)=c_p\Lambda_p^t+O(\rho_p^t),\qquad
  B_q(m)=d_qK_q^m+O(\sigma_q^m),
  \quad p\in P,\ q\in Q,
\]
with every coefficient and error bound supplied by the effective packages.
Let \(E_U\) and \(E_V\) be the finite sets of values represented by all
zero-pump loops and by every parameter discarded in forming these packages,
and put \(E=E_U\cup E_V\). These sets are computed by direct evaluation.

\begin{theorem}[Effective cardinality bound]
  \label{thm:effective-slender-cfl-cardinality}
  From an effective two-system presentation for \(X\), one can compute an
  upper bound for \(\abs X\). More precisely, set
  \[
    M_{pq}=M(A_p,B_q),\qquad N_{pq}=M(B_q,A_p).
  \]
  Then the integer
  \begin{equation}
    \mathcal B=\abs E+
      \sum_{p\in P}\sum_{q\in Q}(M_{pq}N_{pq}+1)
    \label{eq:effective-global-cardinality-bound}
  \end{equation}
  is computable from the presentation and satisfies \(\abs X\le\mathcal B\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  Fix \(p\in P\) and \(q\in Q\). Their dominant roots are positive powers
  of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), respectively, and hence are
  multiplicatively independent. The effective Mignotte thresholds in
  \eqref{eq:mignotte-effective-threshold}, applied in both orders, imply that
  every solution of \(A_p(t)=B_q(m)\) outside
  \[
    0\le t<M_{pq},\qquad 0\le m<N_{pq}
  \]
  satisfies
  \begin{equation}
    c_p\Lambda_p^t=d_qK_q^m.
    \label{eq:effective-leading-term-equality}
  \end{equation}
  Equation \eqref{eq:effective-leading-term-equality} has at most one
  nonnegative integer solution: two distinct solutions would give
  \(
    \Lambda_p^{t_1-t_2}=K_q^{m_1-m_2}
  \), contrary to multiplicative independence. The finite rectangle contains
  at most \(M_{pq}N_{pq}\) pairs. Therefore
  \[
    \#\{(t,m):A_p(t)=B_q(m)\}\le M_{pq}N_{pq}+1.
  \]

  If \(x\in X\setminus E\), its unique \(U\)-representation lies in the
  retained tail of some \(U\)-loop and its unique \(V\)-representation lies
  in the retained tail of some \(V\)-loop. Thus \(x=A_p(t)=B_q(m)\) for some
  \(p,q,t,m\). Summing the pair bounds and adding \(E\) gives
  \eqref{eq:effective-global-cardinality-bound}. Repeated values or overlap
  among loops are only overcounted.
\end{proof}

The input to \(\mathcal B\) is the full recurrence and loop data: it includes
the individual recurrence thresholds and initial values, the actual fixed
and pumped words, the affine and tensor matrices, the algebraic dominant
coefficients, spectral gaps, and Mignotte's effective constants. We do not
extract a closed expression in grammar size, recurrence heights, or block
lengths. In particular, no uniformity is being inferred from the finitely
many prefixes: each discarded prefix and each shift \(s_r\) is computed and
entered in \(E\).

\begin{remark}[Priority and scope]
  \label{rem:slender-cobham-priority}
  Three existing Cobham statements delimit the result. The natural published
  benchmark for the regular integer-base case is the quantitative
  Cobham--Semenov theorem of Albayrak--Bell. For multiplicatively independent
  integers \(k,\ell\ge2\), they prove that the intersection of a sparse
  \(k\)-automatic subset of \(\mathbb N^d\) and a sparse \(\ell\)-automatic
  subset of \(\mathbb N^d\) is finite, with an explicit bound in terms of the
  bases, dimension, and minimal automata
  \cite[Theorems~1.1 and 4.1]{AlbayrakBell2023}. Taking the two sets equal gives
  simultaneous sparse automatic finiteness. A slender regular integer-base
  representation language is sparse, so this contains the regular
  integer-base specialization of the theorem above. More broadly, their
  \(d\)-dimensional statement covers sparse automatic tuple sets whose regular
  representation languages may have polynomial rather than bounded word
  growth; in particular it covers the regular poly-slender integer-base
  shadow. Their theorem is strictly stronger on the overlap and broader in
  this regular direction. The effective result above computes a cardinality
  bound from the complete recurrence and paired-loop data, but it does not
  close the quantitative gap: Albayrak--Bell give a closed expression in the
  bases, dimension, and numbers of states of the minimal automata. They also
  distinguish that cardinality estimate from the separate task of actually
  computing the intersection; we make the same distinction here.

  Second, Durand proves that a sequence which is simultaneously
  \(\alpha\)- and \(\beta\)-substitutive for multiplicatively independent
  Perron numbers is ultimately periodic
  \cite[Theorem~1]{Durand2011CobhamSubstitutions}. Third, the abstract-
  numeration theorem of Charlier--Leroy--Rigo starts with infinite regular
  languages ordered genealogically, requires both representation languages
  of the set to be regular, and concludes that simultaneous recognition in
  two independent systems gives a finite union of arithmetic progressions
  \cite[Definitions~33, 34, and 47 and Theorem~49]%
  {CharlierLeroyRigo2013CobhamANS}. In its exponential case, independence
  means multiplicative independence of the dominant language-growth
  eigenvalues. Thus the regular Perron-substitutive and regular abstract-
  numeration shadows are already part of existing Cobham theory.

  Those recognition hypotheses fail at the full scope of the theorem above.
  A slender context-free representation language may be genuinely
  nonregular, so it need not furnish either a finite automaton recognizing
  the full representation language or a substitutive characteristic
  sequence. The dimension in Albayrak--Bell does not remove this condition:
  a coordinate or product encoding enters their theorem only when its padded
  synchronous tuple language is itself sparse regular, and its coordinates
  still use ordinary integer-base valuation. It therefore does not absorb a
  genuinely nonregular paired-loop language or replace the weak-Perron affine
  value map used here. Nor need a weak-Perron positional system supply the
  regular canonical, genealogical-rank interface required by an abstract
  numeration system.
  The role of \Cref{lem:paired-loop-dominant-root-transfer} is precisely the
  nonregular weak-Perron bridge: it sends each word-theoretic paired loop to
  residue subsequences with a unique positive dominant root, while resolving
  peripheral collisions, affine and tensor-product Jordan factors, and
  cancellation by the value functional. Only after that transfer can
  Mignotte's common-value theorem be applied.

  Accordingly, the regular integer-base and regular abstract-numeration
  shadows belong to existing Cobham theory. What is new here is the passage
  from regular recognition to full slender context-free representation
  languages, together with the dominant-root transfer for paired loops in
  weak-Perron positional systems. This claim does not extend to nonregular
  poly-slender representation languages: finite unions of higher Dyck loops
  would require a genuinely multivariate argument, which is not asserted
  here.
\end{remark}

\section{Synchronized pumping and recurrent numeration}
\label{sec:context-free-pisot}

We now pass from finite automata to pushdown automata. Recall that an
infinite language is \emph{CF-immune} if it contains no infinite
context-free sublanguage. Here a context-free language means one accepted
by an arbitrary nondeterministic pushdown automaton, equivalently generated
by a context-free grammar. We impose no determinism, unambiguity,
real-time, or growth hypothesis on that automaton. The classical
fixed-base theorem is due independently to Hartmanis--Shank and
Sch\"utzenberger
\cite{HartmanisShank1968,Schutzenberger1968}. The point below is that
the square-modulus block action survives the two simultaneous pumps
supplied by Ogden's lemma \cite{Ogden1968}; the interchange lemma of
Ogden--Ross--Winklmann \cite{OgdenRossWinklmann1985} is a stronger
related tool, but is not needed for the proof.

Write
\[
  \mathcal Z=\{x_1\cdots x_m\in\{0,1\}^\ast:
      x_ix_{i+1}\ne11,\ x_m=1\}
\]
and \(\val(x_1\cdots x_m)=\sum_{j=1}^m x_jF_{j+1}\).
For \(n\ge2\), let \(\omega(n)\) and \(\Omega(n)\) denote respectively
the number of distinct prime divisors and the number counted with
  multiplicity; put \(\omega(1)=\Omega(1)=0\).

\begin{lemma}[Unimodular Zeckendorf block action]
  \label{lem:main-zeckendorf-unimodular-block-action}
  After an LSD-first prefix \(x_1\cdots x_r\), put
  \[
    V_r=\begin{pmatrix}N_r\\F_{r+1}\\F_{r+2}\end{pmatrix},
    \qquad N_r=\sum_{j=1}^r x_jF_{j+1},
    \qquad V_0=(0,1,1)^t.
  \]
  Reading \(\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}\) sends \(V_r\) to
  \[
    D_\varepsilon V_r,
    \qquad
    D_\varepsilon=
    \begin{pmatrix}
      1&0&\varepsilon\\
      0&0&1\\
      0&1&1
    \end{pmatrix},
    \qquad \det D_\varepsilon=-1.
  \]
  For a block \(y=y_1\cdots y_\ell\), therefore,
  \(M_y=D_{y_\ell}\cdots D_{y_1}\) has determinant
  \((-1)^\ell\), concatenation acts by multiplication of the block
  matrices, and every nonempty \(M_y\) belongs to
  \(\operatorname{GL}_3(\ZZ/q\ZZ)\) for every \(q\ge2\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
  The identities
  \[
    N_{r+1}=N_r+\varepsilon F_{r+2},\qquad
    F_{r+2}=F_{r+2},\qquad F_{r+3}=F_{r+1}+F_{r+2}
  \]
  give the displayed action. Expanding along the first row gives
  \(\det D_\varepsilon=-1\); the remaining assertions follow by
  multiplication and reduction modulo \(q\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Paired Zeckendorf pumping congruence]
  \label{lem:zeckendorf-paired-pumping-congruence}
  Let \(u,v,x,y,z\in\{0,1\}^\ast\), and put
  \[
    N(k):=\val(uv^kxy^kz)\qquad(k\ge0).
  \]
  Suppose that \(\abs v+\abs y>0\). If \(q\ge2\), and \(h\) is a
  common multiple of the orders modulo \(q\) of the nonempty-block
  matrices among \(M_v,M_y\) (with \(M_\varepsilon=I\)), then
  \[
    N(k+h)\equiv N(k)\pmod q
    \qquad(k\ge0).
  \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
  With \(v_0=(0,1,1)^t\), concatenation and
  \Cref{lem:main-zeckendorf-unimodular-block-action} give
  \[
    N(k)=e_1^tM_zM_y^kM_xM_v^kM_uv_0.
  \]
  Every nonempty block matrix is invertible modulo \(q\). By the
  definition of \(h\), both \(M_v^h\equiv I\pmod q\) and
  \(M_y^h\equiv I\pmod q\), where the same identities are automatic for
  an empty block. Substitution in the displayed product proves the
  congruence.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Context-free coprime-quotient Zeckendorf pumping]
  \label{thm:context-free-coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping}
  Let \(L\subseteq\mathcal Z\) be context-free. There is an integer
  \(P_L\ge1\) such that every \(w\in L\) with
  \(\abs w\ge P_L\) and \(\val(w)\ge2\) begins a sequence
  \(w_0=w,w_1,w_2,\ldots\) in \(L\) whose lengths are strictly
  increasing and whose values \(N_i=\val(w_i)\) satisfy
  \[
    N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i,\qquad Q_i>1,\qquad
    Q_i\equiv1\pmod {N_i},\qquad \gcd(Q_i,N_i)=1.
  \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  Apply Ogden's lemma with every position distinguished. It supplies a
  constant \(P_L\) such that each \(w\in L\) of length at least \(P_L\)
  has a factorisation
  \[
    w=uvxyz,\qquad \abs v+\abs y>0,\qquad
    uv^kxy^kz\in L\quad(k\ge0).
  \]
  The additional marked-position bound in Ogden's lemma is not needed
  here. Starting with \(w_i\in L\), choose such a factorisation and
  let \(h_i\) be a common multiple of the orders of \(M_v\) and \(M_y\)
  in
  \(\operatorname{GL}_3(\ZZ/N_i^2\ZZ)\), omitting an empty block. These
  orders exist by
  \Cref{lem:main-zeckendorf-unimodular-block-action}. Define
  \[
    w_{i+1}:=uv^{\,1+h_i}xy^{\,1+h_i}z.
  \]
  By \Cref{lem:zeckendorf-paired-pumping-congruence},
  \(N_{i+1}\equiv N_i\pmod {N_i^2}\). Hence
  \(N_{i+1}=N_i(1+t_iN_i)\) for an integer \(t_i\).

  Since \(h_i\ge1\) and \(\abs v+\abs y>0\), the new word is longer.
  Both words belong to \(L\subseteq\mathcal Z\), and canonical
  Zeckendorf intervals are strictly ordered by length; consequently
  \(N_{i+1}>N_i\), so \(t_i\ge1\). Taking
  \(Q_i=1+t_iN_i\) gives all four assertions. The new word still has
  length at least \(P_L\) and value at least \(2\), so the construction
  iterates.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Zeckendorf CF-immunity package]
  \label{cor:zeckendorf-context-free-immunity-package}
  Every infinite context-free \(L\subseteq\mathcal Z\) satisfies
  \[
    \sup_{w\in L}\omega(\val(w))=\infty.
  \]
  Consequently, for each \(K\ge1\), the bounded-distinct-prime language
  \(\mathcal B_K\), the bounded-almost-prime language \(\mathcal A_K\),
  and every infinite finite-prime-support language \(\mathcal Z_S\)
  are CF-immune. In particular, the Zeckendorf prime language
  \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal Z}\) is CF-immune.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Arbitrarily deep quotient congruences]
  \label{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain}
  Suppose \(\abs{a_0}=1\), and let \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) be an
  infinite MCFL. For arbitrary sequences \(M_i\ge1\) and \(r_i\ge1\),
  \(L\) contains a strictly increasing sequence \(N_i\) such that
  \[
    N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i,\qquad Q_i>1,\qquad
    Q_i\equiv1\pmod {M_iN_i^{r_i}}.
  \]
  If \(M_i\) is divisible by every prime at most \(B_i\), then every
  prime divisor of \(Q_i\) exceeds \(B_i\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  Take the fixed orbit \(N(t)\) from
  \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}, discarding finitely many
  initial parameters so that \(N(t)\ge2\). Having selected
  \(N_i=N(t_i)\), apply the synchronized congruence with
  \[
    q_i=M_iN_i^{r_i+1}.
  \]
  The values \(N(t_i+mH(q_i))\), \(m\ge1\), are pairwise distinct and all
  are congruent to \(N_i\) modulo \(q_i\). Only finitely many positive
  integers are at most \(N_i\), so choose \(m_i\ge1\) for which
  \(N(t_i+m_iH(q_i))>N_i\), and set
  \(t_{i+1}=t_i+m_iH(q_i)\). The congruence gives
  \[
    N_{i+1}=N_i+c_iM_iN_i^{r_i+1}
           =N_i(1+c_iM_iN_i^{r_i})
  \]
  for an integer \(c_i\ge1\). This proves the first assertion. Under
  the last hypothesis, \(Q_i\equiv1\pmod p\) for every prime
  \(p\le B_i\), so none of those primes divides \(Q_i\).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Induced full divisibility tree]
  \label{thm:unit-mcfl-divisibility-tree}
  Under the hypotheses of
  \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain}, there is an injection
  \[
    \Phi:\NN^{<\omega}\longrightarrow L
  \]
  such that
  \[
    \val_U(\Phi(\sigma))\mid\val_U(\Phi(\tau))
      \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma\preceq\tau,
  \]
  where \(\preceq\) denotes the prefix order. The quotients attached to
  distinct edges can be chosen pairwise coprime. Moreover, given an
  arbitrary prescribed threshold for each edge, every prime divisor of
  its quotient can be required to exceed that threshold.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  Use the fixed pairwise-distinct orbit from
  \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}. Here is an explicit
  parent-before-child enumeration. If \(p_i\) is the \(i\)-th prime, encode
  \(\sigma=(\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_{m-1})\) by
  \[
    \kappa(\sigma)=2^m\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}p_{i+2}^{\sigma_i+1}.
  \]
  Unique factorization makes \(\kappa\) injective, and
  \(\kappa(\sigma^\frown j)>\kappa(\sigma)\). Enumerating the nonroot
  nodes, equivalently their incoming edges, by increasing \(\kappa\)
  therefore has order type \(\omega\) and places every parent before each
  child. Map
  the root to any orbit word of value \(R_0\ge2\). Suppose finitely many
  edges have been assigned, and consider a new edge from a parent of
  value \(P\). Let \(R\) be divisible by \(R_0\), by every previously
  assigned edge quotient, and by every prime not exceeding the prescribed
  threshold for the new edge. Apply the synchronized orbit congruence
  modulo \(P^2R\) at the parameter of the parent. Positive multiples of
  the return time give pairwise distinct positive values in the indicated
  congruence class. Only finitely many are at most \(P\), so some multiple
  gives an unused orbit word of value \(P'>P\) with
  \[
    P'\equiv P\pmod {P^2R}.
  \]
  Hence \(P'=PQ\), where \(Q>1\) and \(Q\equiv1\pmod {PR}\). In
  particular, \(Q\) is coprime to the root and to every earlier edge
  quotient, and no prime up to the prescribed threshold divides \(Q\).

  Recursion defines \(\Phi\) on every node. The value at a node is the
  root value times the product of the edge quotients along its path.
  Since the root and all distinct edge quotients are pairwise coprime,
  the value at \(\sigma\) divides the value at \(\tau\) exactly when the
  root-to-\(\sigma\) edge set is contained in the root-to-\(\tau\) edge
  set. For two nodes of a rooted tree, containment of their root-path edge
  sets holds exactly when the first node is an ancestor of the second;
  here this is precisely \(\sigma\preceq\tau\). This also proves injectivity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Prime immunity for recurrent numeration systems]
  \label{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity}
  Let \((U,A,\mathcal R_U)\) satisfy \textup{(U1)}, \textup{(U2)}, and
  \textup{(U4)}, and put
  \[
    \mathcal P_U
      :=\{w\in\mathcal R_U:\val_U(w)\text{ is prime}\}.
  \]
  Then \(\mathcal P_U\) is MCF-immune, and therefore CF-immune,
  REG-immune, and not recognizable by a finite automaton over \(A\).

  If, in addition, \(\abs{a_0}=1\), then every infinite multiple
  context-free
  \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) has unbounded
  \(\omega(\val_U(w))\). More precisely, \(L\) contains a
  coprime-quotient chain \(N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i\) with
  \(Q_i>1\) and \(Q_i\equiv1\pmod {N_i}\). Thus the bounded-\(\omega\),
  bounded-\(\Omega\), and finite-prime-support languages of a unit
  system are MCF-immune whenever they are infinite. Without the unit
  hypothesis, every bounded-\(\Omega\) language is still MCF-immune.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
  The MCF-immunity assertions follow from
  \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}, including its
  bounded-\(\Omega\) conclusion. In a unit system \(S\) is empty, so
  that theorem gives unbounded \(\omega\). Taking
  \(M_i=r_i=1\) in
  \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} gives the stated chain.
  Regular languages are context-free and context-free languages are
  MCFLs. Finally, \textup{(U2)} and Euclid's theorem make
  \(\mathcal P_U\) infinite.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Greedy length interval.}
For a standard greedy linear numeration basis with \(U_0=1\), a positive
integer has a canonical greedy word of length \(m\) if and only if it lies
in the half-open interval
\[
  [U_{m-1},U_m).
\]
Indeed, the greedy algorithm chooses the least threshold \(U_m\) strictly
larger than the represented integer; minimality of \(m\) gives the lower
bound, and the choice of \(U_m\) gives the upper bound. This is a property
of the standard greedy subclass, not an assumption on the ambient
canonical eventually recurrent systems.

\begin{corollary}[Linear numeration bases with Perron recurrence]
  \label{cor:linear-perron-prime-cf-immunity}
  Let \(U=(U_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a standard greedy linear numeration basis in
  the following precise sense: \(U_0=1\), the \(U_n\) are strictly
  increasing integers with bounded quotients, \(\mathcal R_U\) is the LSD-first
  reversal of the usual greedy representation language, and \(U\)
  has minimal tail recurrence polynomial equal to the minimal polynomial
  of a Perron number \(\beta\). Thus
  \(\beta>1\) is a real algebraic integer and every other conjugate
  \(\beta'\) satisfies \(\abs{\beta'}<\beta\); compare
  \cite{LindMarcus1995,Rigo2014Vol2}. Then its prime
  representation language is MCF-immune, hence CF-immune, REG-immune and
  nonrecognizable. The same statements hold in the usual MSD-first
  convention.

  If the dominant Perron number is a unit and the chosen recurrence has
  trailing coefficient \(a_0=\pm1\), then the full coprime-quotient and
  bounded-prime-support MCF-immunity conclusions of
  \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity} hold.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
  Greedy expansion gives a unique representation of every positive
  integer, and its length-\(m\) words represent values between successive
  place-value thresholds; thus \textup{(U1)} and \textup{(U2)} hold. The defining
  Perron recurrence gives \textup{(U4)}. Apply
  \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity}. The immunity proof
  uses only \textup{(U1)}, \textup{(U2)}, and \textup{(U4)} and does not
  assume that the full greedy language is regular. In the Pisot subclass,
  Frougny's finite
  normalization theorem supplies a finite transducer, and the associated
  canonical syntax and Bertrand/substitution descriptions are standard
  \cite{Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,Fabre1995,FrougnySolomyak1992}.
  Finally, multiple context-free, context-free, and
  regular languages are closed under reversal, so changing between the LSD-first proof
  convention and the usual MSD-first convention preserves every
  conclusion.
\end{proof}
